## 1. Identification Strategy  

Instrumental‐Variables (shift–share / “Bartik-style”) combined with a difference-in-differences/event-study at the county–year level.

• First stage (supply shock): predict the change in small-business lending to county *c* in year *t* with the weighted average pre-crisis real-estate exposure of the banks that historically lent in that county.  
• Second stage: estimate the effect of the (instrumented) change in small-business credit on county-level employment/output.

Why IV?  
– Pure DiD (“high- vs low-exposed counties before/after 2008”) is vulnerable to demand shocks that are correlated with bank exposure.  
– A bank-level instrument that varies within counties over time allows us to difference out local demand and isolate credit-supply movements that originate inside bank balance sheets.

## 2. Treatment and Control  

Treatment variable (endogenous regressor)  
Lend_ct  ≡  log of CRA small-business loan originations (or $\Delta$ log) in county *c*, year *t*.

Instrument (shift–share)  
Shock_ct  =  Σ_b  (Share_{cb,2006} × RE_Expo_b × Post_t)  

where  
• Share_{cb,2006}: fraction of county *c*’s small-business loans in 2006 originated by bank *b*.  
• RE_Expo_b: pre-crisis (2006:Q4) ratio of real-estate-related assets (1–4 mortgages + construction loans + MBS) to total assets for bank *b*.  
• Post_t = 1{t ≥ 2008}.  

Control / counterfactual  
Counties whose historical lenders had low RE_Expo_b receive small (near-zero) Shock_ct values and therefore serve as the implicit control group in the 2SLS framework.

Timing  
Pre-period: 2004–2007 (stable credit market).  
Post-period: 2008–2010 (crisis / early recovery).

## 3. Key Identifying Assumptions  

A1. Relevance – Banks with higher RE_Expo_b cut lending more after 2008 (strong first stage).  
Plausible: well documented that MBS/construction losses impaired bank capital.

A2. Exclusion – Conditional on county and year fixed effects (and controls), pre-crisis RE_Expo_b affects county employment/output only through its impact on small-business credit supply, not via local demand.  
Plausibility strengthened by:
  • Using *pre-crisis* exposure.  
  • Weighting by 2006 loan shares, predetermined relative to crisis.  
  • Controlling directly for local housing price changes and foreclosure rates.

A3. Parallel trends / no differential pre-trends – Treated and control counties followed similar employment paths pre-2008 once we control for county FEs and linear trends.  
We will test via event-study coefficients on leads of Shock_ct.

A4. Stable shares – 2006 loan shares proxy for the intensity with which each bank serves a county and are exogenous to post-crisis shocks.  
Reasonable because lending relationships in CRA data are sticky; we also show results using 2005 and averaged 2004-06 shares.

A5. SUTVA / no spillovers – A bank’s balance-sheet shock does not directly alter employment in counties where the bank had no pre-crisis presence.  
Plausible given limited cross-county reallocation of small-business lending in short run.

## 4. Threats to Identification & Mitigations  

T1. Local demand shocks correlated with bank exposure (e.g., counties with bigger housing busts both lost jobs and had banks heavy in real-estate lending).  
Mitigation:  
– Add county-level controls: ∆ house prices, foreclosure rates, construction employment share.  
– Include commuting-zone × year fixed effects so variation is within CZ.  
– Placebo test: interact RE_Expo_b with pre-2008 years; coefficients should be ≈0.

T2. Measurement error in CRA small-business lending (not all banks report or misclassify).  
Mitigation:  
– Aggregate all banks’ CRA filings.  
– Winsorize extreme loan values.  
– Repeat using Call Report C&I loan growth where available.

T3. Bank selection / branch network changes 2006–2010.  
Mitigation:  
– Use fixed 2006 shares.  
– Drop counties where market‐entry/exit of large banks is observed (robustness).  
– Alternative instrument: national average mortgage-default rate × RE_Expo_b (“national shock”) aggregated by 2006 shares.

## 5. R Code Outline  

```r
# Required packages
library(data.table)
library(fixest)    # fast felm / iv
library(ivreg)     # for iv diagnostics
library(lmtest); library(sandwich)

# 1. Load data -------------------------------------------------------------
cra  <- fread("CRA_loans_1996_2010.csv")      # bank-county-year
call <- fread("CallReports_1996_2010.csv")    # bank-quarter
cbp  <- fread("CBP_county_1996_2010.csv")     # county-year
hp   <- fread("Zillow_HPI_1996_2010.csv")     # county-year house prices

# 2. Variable construction -------------------------------------------------
## 2a. Bank-level pre-crisis real-estate exposure (2006Q4)
call_06 <- call[year==2006 & quarter==4,
                .(RE_Expo = (residential_loans + constr_loans + MBS)/total_assets),
                by = bank_id]

## 2b. 2006 loan shares by county
cra_06 <- cra[year==2006, .(loan_amt = sum(sb_loans)), by = .(county, bank_id)]
cra_06[, share := loan_amt / sum(loan_amt), by = county]
cra_06 <- merge(cra_06, call_06, by="bank_id", all.x=TRUE)

## 2c. Build shift–share instrument for all years
years <- 2004:2010
panel <- CJ(county = unique(cra$county), year = years)  # skeleton

# attach instrument
ss_mat <- dcast(cra_06, county ~ bank_id, value.var="share", fill=0)
re_vec <- call_06$RE_Expo; names(re_vec) <- call_06$bank_id
ss_mat_long <- melt(ss_mat, id="county", variable.name="bank_id", value.name="share")
ss_mat_long[, RE_Expo := re_vec[as.character(bank_id)]]
ss_mat_long[, weight := share * RE_Expo]

Z <- ss_mat_long[, .(Z = sum(weight)), by = county]      # time-invariant component
panel <- merge(panel, Z, by="county", all.x=TRUE)
panel[, Post := as.integer(year >= 2008)]
panel[, Shock := Z * Post]                               # instrument

## 2d. Dependent variables
cra_ct <- cra[, .(lend = sum(sb_loans)), by = .(county, year)]
cbp_ct <- cbp[, .(emp = sum(emp_total)), by = .(county, year)]
hp_ct  <- hp[, .(hp_change = 100*(log(hpi) - shift(log(hpi))), by=county)]

panel <- Reduce(function(d1,d2) merge(d1,d2, all.x=TRUE, by=c("county","year")),
                list(panel, cra_ct, cbp_ct, hp_ct))
panel[, c("log_lend","log_emp") := .(log(1+lend), log(emp))]

# 3. Main IV specification -------------------------------------------------
# county & year fixed effects, robust clustered SEs
iv_main <- feols(log_emp ~ 1 | county + year | 
                 (log_lend ~ Shock) | 0,
                 data = panel, cluster = "county")
summary(iv_main)

# First-stage F-stat
etable(iv_main, stage = 1)

# 4. Robustness: add county housing-price control and CZ×year FE -----------
panel[, cz := substr(county,1,5)]               # assume first 5 digits = CZ
iv_rob <- feols(log_emp ~ hp_change | cz^year + county | 
                (log_lend ~ Shock) | 0,
                data = panel, cluster = "cz")
summary(iv_rob)
```

## 6. Expected Results  

Theory: When banks shrink credit supply, small firms—especially in credit-dependent counties—cut jobs quickly.

Back-of-the-envelope prior  
• Elasticity ≈ 0.2–0.3: a 10 percent (log-point) decline in small-business lending leads to ≈2–3 percent fall in county small-firm employment within one year.  
• Aggregate county employment effect smaller (≈0.5 percent) because small firms are only part of the labor force.

## 7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV)  

C1: Strong first stage (F-stat > 10) ………………… 1  
C2: Exclusion (instrument affects Y only via X) …… 0.7  
C3: No differential pre-trends / placebo leads …… 0.8  
C4: Stable shares (no endogenous exposure) ……… 0.8  
C5: No large spillovers / SUTVA  …………………… 0.7  

Average ≈ 0.8 → credible but not bullet-proof.
